OpenRouter Warns MiniMax Prompts May Have Been Read by a Third Party

OpenRouter warned MiniMax users their prompts may have been read; the Zero Data Retention label described the first hop, not the whole chain.

ISSUE 462 · 2026-11-21 · SOURCE / RSS Feeds Cloud · STATUS / VERIFIED · TOKENTA SIGNAL RESEARCH
OPENROUTER × MINIMAX × DATA RETENTIONREPORTED + ANALYSIS
40–130 hours
THE DELAY
Delay before test links planted in MiniMax prompts were opened by a third party, long after inference had finished.
3 providers
THE FORWARDERS
Forwarding providers, AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake, that passed OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax.
~2M prompts
THE STUDY
Canary prompts HD Moore's team sent through AI services between July and November 2026 to test where secrets surfaced.
KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • 01THE TEST — July-October 2026: unique test URLs planted in prompts sent to MiniMax models.
  • 02THE SIGNAL — 40-130 hours later: a third party opens the links, long after inference finished.
  • 03THE WARNING — November 21: OpenRouter emails affected customers; the email circulates on Hacker News.

WHAT HAPPENEDWhat Happened

On November 21, 2026, an email from OpenRouter began circulating on Hacker News under the subject line "Requests you sent to MiniMax models may have been read." One recipient posted it in full, and Max Woolf, the researcher known online as minimaxir, confirmed he had received the same message independently. The email says a security researcher placed unique test URLs inside prompts sent to MiniMax models between July and October 2026, and a third party opened those URLs 40 to 130 hours after the requests were sent. It happened whether MiniMax served the request directly or another provider forwarded it to MiniMax. The notices were personalized to each recipient's own history: one developer's copy listed 321 requests to MiniMax models sent through four providers, MiniMax itself, Novita, StreamLake and AtlasCloud, between June 6 at 09:16 UTC and October 22 at 06:48 UTC.

The researcher behind the email is HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at Dragos. In a writeup published November 19, covered the next day by Ars Technica, Moore describes sending roughly two million prompts carrying unique, trackable secrets through widely used AI services between July and November 2026, then watching where those secrets surfaced. Dragos anonymizes the companies in its report, but the finding it describes matches OpenRouter's notification closely: the lab's systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of those explicitly marked no-data-collection or Zero Data Retention, and the scraper typically appeared two to three days after the request. A git client on a different cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, again only for prompts that used that lab's models.

The response draws the line between the router and the model. AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake told OpenRouter they forwarded OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax, and OpenRouter says the issue sits with MiniMax and the forwarding providers, not with OpenRouter itself. MiniMax told StreamLake that content moderation was enabled on its endpoints before October 22 and that it has since enabled Zero Data Retention; OpenRouter asked MiniMax for its own account and had not received one. While it investigates, OpenRouter removed the Zero Data Retention label from the affected MiniMax endpoints, and its provider table now lists MiniMax, AtlasCloud and StreamLake alike as retaining prompts for an unknown period while not training on them. Two details limit the damage: with one exception, the same tests run against other models at those same providers were never accessed, and none of the researcher's AWS test keys were used. No credentials were stolen. But the public record does not establish who or what performed the fetches, or on whose instructions.

WHY IT MATTERSA label is not a boundary

The uncomfortable finding is structural. Zero Data Retention at OpenRouter is endpoint metadata assembled from provider agreements and attestations, and the platform does not independently verify upstream behavior. A privacy flag binds only the first hop: the router reads plaintext to decide where a request goes, the host reads plaintext to run inference, and a forwarder can quietly pass the request on to the model developer under another company's policy. Dragos concluded that a customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep data in the United States did not get what they paid for. MiniMax is headquartered in Shanghai and listed in Hong Kong in January 2026, and its international API is operated by a Singapore-registered entity, but the customer who chose a San Francisco or New York provider under a ZDR label never chose MiniMax at all.

The industry has already been renegotiating what zero means. On October 18, Google began requiring Safety Retention for models served through Vertex, and on October 26 OpenRouter formalized Safety Retention as a third policy tier between ZDR and retention-and-training. The MiniMax case shows why that renegotiation is not academic: a label that describes the endpoint a customer selects says nothing about where the request goes next, and no per-request visibility exists, on OpenRouter or anywhere else, to tell a customer that a completion labeled ZDR would run on another company's infrastructure under another company's policy.

WHAT TO WATCHWhat to watch after the warning

Watch for MiniMax's own account, which OpenRouter says it has requested and not received, and for whether OpenRouter publishes a public incident page; as of the Hacker News posting, the email was the only disclosure. Watch whether other routers audit their forwarding chains, and whether enterprise customers demand contractual guarantees that cover the whole chain rather than the first hop. The stronger control already exists for customers who need location rather than retention: in-region routing through OpenRouter's US and EU domains, where prompts and completions are processed entirely within the region.

Watch also for the rest of the Dragos study. The MiniMax finding is one strand of a five-month experiment that sent about two million canary prompts through widely used services, and the writeup describes three providers breached without their knowledge and resellers logging prompts. If further strands name names the way OpenRouter's email named MiniMax, the ZDR label itself, not just one lab's endpoints, will be on trial.

THE SHIFTWhat Changed

FROM LABEL TO TEST
From a privacy label to a canary test
Zero Data Retention was a metadata flag assembled from provider attestations. A canary experiment that plants unique links in prompts tested what actually happened to the data, and the flag failed the test.
FROM FIRST HOP TO FULL CHAIN
From first hop to full chain
OpenRouter's routing enforces policy at the endpoint a customer selects. The MiniMax path shows the request can quietly continue to another company's infrastructure under another company's policy.

SIGNAL JUDGMENT — ANALYSISOpenRouter Warns MiniMax Prompts May Have Been Read by a Third Party

Tokenta Signal's judgment: The uncomfortable finding is not that a lab kept prompts; it is that the privacy label customers relied on described only the first hop. OpenRouter's email is unusually candid about that: its ZDR flag reflects provider attestations, not independently verified behavior, and three providers forwarded requests to MiniMax without the customer ever seeing it. The exposure looks bounded, no credentials were used and other models at the same providers were untouched, but the structural lesson travels far beyond MiniMax. Any router that forwards to third-party infrastructure is only as private as its least visible hop, and the only controls that survive that are the ones that constrain the whole chain.

WHAT REMAINS UNCERTAINWhat Remains Uncertain

OpenRouter's email is the disclosure; as of the Hacker News posting there was no public blog post or incident page from OpenRouter, and MiniMax has not published its own account. The Dragos study anonymizes the companies it tested; OpenRouter names MiniMax. The public record does not establish who or what performed the fetches. This article is a summary with links only and does not reproduce any source text. This does not constitute investment advice.

EVIDENCEEvidence

OpenRouter emailed customers on November 21, 2026, warning that prompts and outputs sent to MiniMax models may have been read by a third party. Researcher HD Moore planted unique test URLs in prompts between July and October 2026; a third party opened them 40 to 130 hours later. OpenRouter removed the Zero Data Retention label from the affected MiniMax endpoints while it awaits MiniMax's own account.
